source.title: AlignSAE: Concept-Aligned Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Minglai Yang; Xin-Yu Guo; Zheng-Liang Shi; Jin-He Bi; Steven Bethard; Mihai Surdeanu; Liangming Pan

record.file_problem: none; full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports results comparing unsupervised SAE features with concept-supervised slots, and explicitly cautions that the one-to-one slot mapping is imposed by supervision rather than necessarily reflecting the model's native representation. This refines claims about SAE features as model units; it does not reproduce the toy-model superposition experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses superposition and polysemanticity in its introduction and cites prior work, but those statements are not results of this study. The relevant results are its own measurements of concept–slot alignment, feature fragmentation/concentration, and MIG. Other reported outcomes, such as generation fluency and perplexity, do not directly measure the claim versions.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper. It proposes AlignSAE, which trains SAE slots under supervision so that each predefined relation concept gets its own slot. Almost every row reports how well that method binds, generalises or steers, with the one-to-one structure imposed by the training loss. The authors say the mapping is a product of the objective, not necessarily the model's native structure. That is a deliberately induced outcome, not a measurement of superposition or of native SAE features. The only non-method numbers are standard-SAE baselines for the same task metrics (fragmentation, Top1C, MIG, swap success). They measure alignment to a human relation ontology, not whether features are sparse or superposed (V4), or complete, stable and canonical (V5). No toy-model, capacity or dimensionality test is reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that supervised SAE post-training creates ontology-aligned slots that are interpretable and steerable in their GPT-2 tasks, with a mid-layer sweet spot. The slot mapping is imposed by supervision, and binding is not full causal control in 2-hop (7.86% swap success). The paper also reports a grokking-like shift from entangled to diagonal binding. Its headline 1-hop swap figure of 94.8% conflicts with the 0.847 in Table 1.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains an SAE on activations from a fine-tuned GPT-2, then post-trains it with concept-binding, orthogonality, and answer-value objectives. It does not use the original toy-network feature generation or geometry measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Binding and controllability vary with layer: layer 6 performs much better than layer 0. In 1-hop, swap success varies with intervention strength: at layer 6 it is 0.54 at α=1, 0.85 at α=2, and 0.23 at α=10. Results also depend on whether concept supervision is used and on task depth.

fits_no_version.finding: In a standard reconstruction-plus-sparsity SAE on fine-tuned GPT-2, each human-defined relation concept spreads over hundreds to thousands of latents, with Top1C ≈ 0 and MIG 0.000. Steering with standard-SAE directions in the 2-hop task gives about 1.5–2.7% swap success.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unsupervised SAE latents do not align one-to-one with predefined human concept categories (here, relation types) in a small fine-tuned LM.

record.problems: The evaluation is limited to a single GPT-2 architecture and synthetic or templated tasks; the authors note that highly indirect LLM-generated questions can exceed the base model's QA capacity. Most results concern concept slots shaped by explicit supervision, not the model's unsupervised native feature geometry. The text reports no uncertainty estimates for the main results.
record.rows_left_out: No otherwise relevant numeric rows were omitted. The paper's results on steering side effects, free-form generation quality, and perplexity were left out because they do not directly measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: No toy networks, no sparsity or importance sweep, no geometry measurements.
No test of capacity competition or of dedicated versus shared dimensions.
No study of what causes polysemantic neurons.

No measurement of features spread across neurons, or of sparse features recovered by an unsupervised SAE, in pretrained LLMs. The SAEs are applied to a GPT-2 fine-tuned on synthetic data, and the evaluation targets supervised alignment.
No test of completeness, stability across seeds or sizes, or canonicity of SAE features.
No comparison of 1-D and multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: The record linked every row to V4 and labelled V4 supported. That treats the method's success at imposing concept slots as evidence about native superposition. The authors explicitly disclaim this, so all links are reset to none and no verdicts are given. There are internal inconsistencies: 1-hop swap is given as 94.8% and as 0.847, and the 2-hop ratio over the standard SAE as 4× and as 2.9×. Superposition is mentioned only in the introduction and related work, with citations.

versions.untested_parts: No small toy networks, feature-sparsity sweep, importance sweep, or test of overlapping nearly orthogonal directions.
No test of capacity competition, feature importance, or dedicated versus shared dimensions as an explanation of neuron polysemanticity.
No study of polysemantic neurons arising through mechanisms other than capacity pressure.

The study measures relation concepts in a fine-tuned GPT-2 on synthetic, templated tasks, not general feature representations in pretrained LLMs on natural corpora. Most tested SAE features are explicitly trained or evaluated against concept labels.

No direct evaluation of whether SAE features are complete, stable across training runs or settings, or canonical units. The authors state that the supervised slot mapping need not reflect the model's native representational structure.
No comparison of one-dimensional directions with multidimensional features. The method assigns scalar slots and intervenes along decoded directions, but does not test feature dimensionality.

relation.reason: The method uses sparse dictionaries motivated by superposition. §3 explicitly distinguishes its supervised slot mapping from the model's native representation.

tranche.reason: The rows report AlignSAE and comparator performance. Concept-slot alignment is explicitly imposed by supervised training; the paper does not test whether the catalog's superposition claims hold.

source_check.notes: All rows are method-performance or comparator results, not direct claim tests. Source inconsistencies remain: §5.2 defines metrics over six slots yet reports hundreds–thousands of effective features and near-zero Top1C; the 2-hop improvement is described as 4× in Fig. 7 and 2.9× in §K.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: GPT-2 on the tested synthetic 1-hop and 2-hop tasks, and the FB15K 91-relation setting, using concept-supervised AlignSAE slots
reader_labels.reason: AlignSAE achieves high concept-slot alignment, including 0.912 unseen-template accuracy at layer 6, 100% step-wise alignment in 2-hop, and 0.757 OOD slot top-1 accuracy on FB15K (R6, R11, R12, R15, R16).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Unsupervised traditional SAE on the study's synthetic GPT-2 tasks; shallow-layer AlignSAE; 2-hop intervention
reader_labels.reason: The traditional SAE has concepts spread over hundreds to thousands of features with Top1C ≈ 0 and 1-hop MIG 0.000; layer-0 binding is weak, and 2-hop swap control remains 7.86% despite strong binding (R1, R7, R8, R10, R13, R14).
